newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina sees no politics in Falkland bid failure.
newsitem.headline: Argentina sees no politics in Falkland bid failure.

text.p: The Argentine government sees no hidden political motives behind YPF's failure to win a Falkland Islands oil exploration license in bid results announced Monday, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
A joint application from Argentine oil giant and British Gas was the only bid that failed.

"But the British government has assured us that the fact that YPF did not get a license responds to purely commercial reasons and that political circumstances did not have any influence," the Argentine official told Reuters.

Argentina accepted the explanation of Andrew Gurr, chief executive of the Falkland Islands government, that the British Gas/YPF bid to explore for oil in waters north of the disputed islands failed "partly because they limited their bidding to the two most successful tranches."
The Argentine diplomat said that YPF had participated in the bidding process, but apparently did not succeed "because its offer was not as good as expected."
He pointed out that Argentine business would be participating via Shell Argentina, a local unit of Royal Dutch/Shell.
"And maybe YPF can work in the area through an agreement with the companies that one licenses. That depends on YPF's commercial interests," said the official.

He said Argentina would still benefit from oil activity around the islands, which it calls the Malvinas and claims as its own territory, through royalties expected to be set at 3.0 percent in a bill now at the committee stage in Congress.

The diplomat said Argentina has a right to royalties on exploration and subsequent extraction in the North Falkland Basin -- seven tranches covering about 12,800 square km -- and the so-called "Special Cooperation Area" straddling the median line between the islands and the Argentine mainland.
Gurr said next licensing round would "almost certainly" cover the Special Cooperation Area.

Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the remote South Atlantic islands in 1982. About 1,000 servicemen, mostly Argentine, died after Britain sent a task force to dislodge troops trying to impose Argentina's sovereignty claim.

The two nations resumed diplomatic ties in 1989 and came to an agreement about cooperation on oil and gas exploration a year ago. Earlier this year they set up a joint committee to administer exploration in Falkland Island waters.
Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella referred to the oil issue in an interview with Reuters last Friday as a "good aspect of the relationship" between the two former foes.
